newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian 1997/98 coffee crop seen sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian 1997/98 coffee crop seen sharply lower.

text.p: Ivory Coast can expect a sharply reduced coffee harvest in 1997/98 (Oct-Sept) after output of 300,000 tonnes in 1996/97, the largest since 367,000 in 1980/81, analysts said on Wednesday.
"It is going to be poor," said one. "There is now enough production on the trees to see."
He added, "It will be much below (1996/97). The (heavy June wet season) rains could help cherry size and improve the situation a bit, but I doubt it."

Ivory Coast had forecast a 1996/97 crop of 230,000 tonnes against 180,000 the previous year. But port arrivals have reached almost 300,000 tonnes -- more than 65 percent up year-on-year -- with three months of the season to go.

Analysts said the 1996/97 crop was a one-off, helped by favourable weather during peak February-March 1996 flowering. The 1997/98 season would confirm a trend towards lower output, despite better maintenance of plantations by farmers.
"This year's crop was absolutely exceptional for Ivory Coast," said one. "The tree stock is old and is definitely taking a rest for next year."
Port arrivals were running at about 2,000 tonnes a week in late June so the final tally for 1996/97 could rise to around 320,000 by the end of the season, said one exporter.
Others said the 1996/97 season had virtually finished, although it is usually officially closed in late September.
"You can consider the season to be be over," one said.

During the mid-1980s, Ivorian crops regularly reached around 280,000 tonnes, before flagging world prices sent yields into a tailspin as farmers neglected trees. Harvests fell to 140-200,000 tonnes in the late 1980s.
In the longer term, harvests could swell as Ivory Coast attempts to fix annual yields at 300,000 tonnes by incentives to farmers, rehabilitation of plantations and replanting.
Few steps have been taken so far, although high farmgate prices in 1995/96 had encouraged farmers to look after trees, analyst said.
A boost could also come from the Interafrican Coffee Organisation's 10-year regional rehabilitation plan.
